item.title: Nvidia wants to 'copy China's homework' and we welcome it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25 01:09:00
Nvidia Photo: VCG While the US is still debating whether "openness is safe," China is building an open, low-cost and decentralized AI ecosystem around the world. This openness reflects a deeper understanding of the very nature of technology. In this sense, if Nvidia treats open source merely as a marketing tool for generating chip orders rather than genuinely committing to building an open, collaborative ecosystem, then the "American DeepSeek" may well turn out to be nothing more than an expensive shell. Several US media outlets recently reported that Nvidia is spending $6 billion to build one of the world's most powerful open-weight AI models, in a bid to compete with Chinese heavyweight models such as DeepSeek and Kimi K3. One of the key contexts behind this move is that most US AI giants have poured far more resources into closed AI models, while the tremendous success of China's open-source models has sparked significant anxiety within the US, making "whether to pivot to open source" a heated topic of debate in the industry. Therefore, Nvidia's turn toward open-weight models has attracted attention. Admittedly, Nvidia's primary motivation is to enter the open-source arena in the face of intense competition, support startups, and thereby secure more chip orders. But objectively speaking, the move is also a sign that the myth of closed-source AI in the US is being further shattered. Previously, the US AI industry was dominated by closed models, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google controlling the closed-source ecosystem. Before the emergence of China's DeepSeek, the market firmly believed that closed source AI is the future. When Chinese open-source models burst onto the scene with low cost, customizability, and local deployability, developers and businesses worldwide suddenly woke up to just how significant the drawbacks of the closed-source models really are. Thus, Nvidia's $6 billion bet on open-source models has led some media to dub it an attempt to build an "American DeepSeek." Notably, the debate over open versus closed source within the US is evolving from a dispute over technical approaches into a contest over strategic direction. Some US political elites and security bureaucrats still cling to the Cold War mentality that "control means security," trying to lock AI technology within their own camp through export controls and investment screening. OpenAI and Anthropic are lobbying vigorously in Washington, urging restrictions on Chinese open-source models and hyping the false narrative of "distillation" - essentially using national security as an excuse to mask their commercial monopoly interests. Because once open-source models match or even surpass closed-source models in performance, their subscription models and application programming interface businesses on which they depend on will face a fundamental challenge. However, faced with China's open-source approach and its increasingly strong capacity for independent innovation, a growing number of people in the US technology industry are realizing that the containment strategy will not only fail to curb the growth of China's open-source ecosystem, but will also cause the US to lose its own competitive edge. Not long ago, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took the rare step of spearheading an open letter on the social media platform in support of open source, prompting Microsoft, Google, Meta and other major players in the industry to publicly voice their support. Several US tech companies have also established the Open Secure AI Alliance (OSAA), which reportedly now has more than 230 members. All of this reflects a broader shift in thinking across the US tech industry. In a sense, Nvidia's $6 billion bet on open source is essentially adding fuel to the open-source movement in the US tech industry. From the attention sparked by DeepSeek to the debut of flagship models such as GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3, the global open-source AI ecosystem, driven largely by Chinese companies, has demonstrated the resilience of this approach and the strength of its development capabilities. In the long run, a thriving open-source community depends on broad participation, transparent mechanisms for collaboration and low barriers to access - not monopolistic investment by any single tech giant. For Nvidia, therefore, whether this money is well spent will depend on chip sales in the short term, model performance in the medium term, and, in the long term, whether it can truly understand the logic of open source. If Nvidia treats open source merely as a marketing tool for generating chip orders rather than genuinely committing to building an open, collaborative ecosystem, then the "American DeepSeek" may well turn out to be nothing more than an expensive shell. Even so, we welcome Nvidia "copying the homework." The value of AI technology lies in making it widely accessible, not keeping it locked away. While the US is still debating whether "openness is safe," China is building an open, low-cost and decentralized AI ecosystem around the world. This openness reflects a deeper understanding of the very nature of technology. Today, open-source models have attracted an ever-growing number of developers worldwide, while countries across the globe are developing their own large language models based on open-source technologies from China. China has demonstrated through concrete actions that openness does not weaken competitiveness; on the contrary, it can give technology greater vitality. As more and more countries choose to join the open ecosystem, the "small yard, high fence" approach will ultimately be swept away by the tide of the times. The ultimate significance of AI lies in enabling every individual and every country to share equally in the benefits of technological progress. From this perspective, open source is not merely a technological approach, but also a choice of values. In the race of open source, the judges are not a handful of Silicon Valley giants, but are the choices of countless developers and users around the world. Nvidia's decision to "copy China's homework" is certainly worth watching, but what matters even more is that a growing number of participants are proving through their actions that openness is the future of AI.

item.title: American teacher revisits land where forest grown from $5,000 donation in 1999
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 23:44:00
Yin Yunzhen introduces to Sakolsky the harvest from the once-barren wasteland. Photo: Lin Xiaoyi/GT On Monday afternoon, American teacher Ronald Sakolsky visited the homeland of Chinese desert fighter Yin Yuzhen in Uxin Banner of Ordos, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. This was a place the American man had visited in 2000 and it has completely changed since then. In 1999, Sakolsky, a teacher in a China-US education exchange program, was touched by a report on Yin and her husband's afforestation efforts in the harsh wilderness of Mu Us Desert, and raised $5,000 to support her green cause. During that visit, they took pictures - in front of the sunken pit where the Yin couple once resided and in the barren land with a finger-thin sapling they had just planted against a backdrop of dust and bare earth. What has the $5,000 changed? On Monday, they came to the Sakolsky forest - a permanent tribute honoring Sakolsky's early contribution to the region's ecological revival - and replicated the vintage pictures, standing in front of a pit that has long been abandoned and beside a newly planted sapling. This time, however, there are bushes and trees in the background. This contrast not only witnessed their friendship across time and the Pacific Ocean, but also showcased a promise Yin has kept for 27 years and a green dream that has been made possible through generations of joint unwavering efforts from Yin, her husband and countless other sand fighters. Homecoming with family cooking Yin hosted Sakolsky on Monday at her home, filling the air with the aroma of home-cooked meals during their long-awaited reunion. Watermelons were served along with other fresh fruits and vegetables, all harvested locally. Yin told the Global Times earlier that she learned the English word "more" to persuade him to eat more. In 1999, Yin had few options for showing her hospitality, so she cooked a bowl of plain noodles for Sakolsky. Now, the harsh wasteland has transformed into a vibrant green oasis, thanks to unwavering afforestation efforts. In the courtyard, the Global Times reporter saw Yin grinning from ear to ear with pride as she introduced the produce from the farmland - green pepper longer than a palm, a bottle gourd even bigger than Yin's head, and bags of foxtail millet packaged with the assistance of Yin's grandchildren, who are proud of the family's generations of commitment to green causes. During a tour of Yin's home, Sakolsky was impressed by the beautiful house with its green courtyard, saying "You deserve every centimeter of this house." Throughout the visit, he repeatedly praised Yin's hands, which the desert fighter and model worker used to change both the land and her own life through arduous work. The $5,000 Sakolsky donated in 1999 was equivalent to three years' income for Yin's entire family at the time. Today, that money has grown into more than 50,000 trees. But Yin's journey did not stop there. Over the following decades, with the support of China's growing ecological restoration policies — including subsidies for afforestation and compensation for forest managers — she transformed the barren land into a productive family forest farm. Her success has inspired many others in the region to take up tree planting and sand control, transforming what was once a desperate struggle into a sustainable livelihood. From the sandy hollow where the Yin couple lived in in 1985 and the earth hut they resided in until 1993, to the solid brick house Sakolsky saw when he last visited, and the two-story house the big family now lives in, the change in living environment is a clear example of ecological dividends. Uxin Banner lies in the heartland of the Mu Us Desert. The desertification rate was over 90 percent in the 1950s and forestation coverage was merely 7.2 percent as of 1980. Now, the forestation rate has increased to 33 percent, while plantation coverage has expanded to 85 percent, per official data. Sakolsky and Yin enjoy watermelons and other fruits at Yin's home. Photo: Lin Xiaoyi/GT Carry on the greenness, kindness This miracle would have been impossible without numerous people like Yin, long-term systematic planning and scientific governance. Chen Ziliang, an expert from the local forestry and grassland bureau, said that Mu Us Desert's sand‑control journey has evolved from collective afforestation to contract desert‑reclamation, moving beyond the simple goal of "keeping trees alive" to restoring vegetation based on water‑resource conditions. Putting the idea of "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" into practice, Uxin Banner no longer views "greenness" and "growth" as an either‑or proposition. On restored sandy lands, the under‑forest economy, eco‑agriculture and eco‑tourism have flourished. Sand‑fixing shrubs are now processed into animal feed and biomass fuel, and local authorities are exploring photovoltaic‑powered desert control, the Global Times learned. Sand control is no longer just about keeping sand away; it's a development approach that guarantees a greener and better living environment alongside a booming economy and increasing incomes. On Monday afternoon, when Sakolsky finally stepped into the forest named after him, this American teacher witnessed the Chinese woman's perseverance and commitment to her promises. The $5,000 donated without expectations has grown into a thriving forest of around 50,000 trees. "A promise is a promise. Ms. Yin fulfilled her promise," Sakolsky said. After 27 years, the wasteland is green, and Sakolsky and Yin are "brother and sister." "This is the answer to how we guide young people: We must teach them love and perseverance. We need to show young people photos of Ms. Yin planting trees, digging the soil with her bare hands," Sakolsky remarked while packing a jar of sand. He said he planned to bring it back to the US, telling his grandchildren it is not just a jar of sand, but "a jar of love." Sakolsky told the Global Times earlier that the younger generation only knows about the dust-covered landscape from photos and stories of the elderly. It is important to tell them how the greenness is achieved, and how every single person can contribute to making an extensive forest in the harshest environment. "I see where China and America can work together. I see it, so I will not quit. She [Yin] never quit. 'Quit' is not in her vocabulary," Sakolsky said with emotion on Monday. "Chinese and Americans can be family. We can get over the differences if we focus on the similarities... If we focus on our similarities and not our differences, we can solve the problems." At the end of Monday's schedule, Yin and Sakolsky planted another sapling together, just as they did about three decades ago, but in a completely different landscape. This new sapling carries on the story of not only greenness through generations of joint efforts, but also kindness across the Pacific Ocean.

item.title: Xi holds talks with Jordan's king; visit empowers development co-op to serve as a pillar of regional stability: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 23:25:00
Photo: Xinhua Chinese President Xi Jinping on Monday held talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing, calling on the two countries to further deepen the alignment of development strategies. The Chinese leader also exchanged views on the situation in the Middle East with the King who is on a state visit to China, which runs through August 18 to 24, the Xinhua News Agency reported. The state visit marks King Abdullah II 's ninth visit to China since his accession to the throne, according to Chinese Foreign Ministry. It takes place more than a decade after the establishment of the strategic partnership between the two nations in 2015 and shortly before the 2027 commemoration of the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations. Following the talks, the two heads of state jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents in areas including diplomacy, economy and trade, industrial and supply chains, and judicial affairs, Xinhua said. The two sides issued a joint statement on deepening the strategic partnership between the two countries, per Xinhua. Upgrading ties The essence of China-Jordan cooperation is mutual benefit and win-win outcomes. China and Jordan should further deepen the alignment of development strategies, Xi said. Both sides should enhance cooperation in traditional fields including economy and trade, infrastructure construction, transportation and mining, expand new drivers of cooperation in digital economy, artificial intelligence and green energy, and comprehensively deepen exchanges in education, culture, science and technology, tourism and other areas, Xi noted, according to Xinhua. Jordan firmly adheres to the one-China policy and recognizes that Taiwan is an integral part of China's territory, the King said, Xinhua reported. The King also noted that Jordan attaches great importance to its relations with China and is committed to deepening cooperation and exchanges with China in areas including economy and trade, manufacturing, agriculture, science and technology, medicine, culture and education. Jordan welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest in the country to achieve common development and prosperity, per Xinhua. Before the top-level engagement in Beijing, King Abdullah II started his China visit in Shanghai and Shenzhen. In Shanghai, the King visited AgiBot, one of China's leading robotics companies, on August 18, followed by discussions on August 19 with representatives from the Trip.com Group, a leading global travel service provider, about strengthening cooperation in tourism sector with China, according to the Jordan News Agency (Petra). During his trip in Shenzhen on August 20, the King visited the T Capital Showcase for Advanced Air Mobility and Robotics in Shenzhen, featuring leading Chinese companies' innovations in robotics, air transport solutions, and logistics services, per a separate Petra report. Wang Jin, an associate professor at the Institute of Middle Eastern Studies at Northwest University in Xi'an, told the Global Times that the King's special trips to Shanghai and Shenzhen to observe scientific‑technological innovation and advanced industries send a positive signal that China‑Jordan cooperation is expanding from traditional economic‑trade, energy and infrastructure collaboration toward scientific‑technological innovation and industrial upgrading. It shows that China‑Jordan strategic partnership is evolving from cooperation in traditional sectors toward all‑round, high‑quality and sustainable collaboration, injecting fresh impetus into the future growth of bilateral ties, Wang added. "China and Middle‑Eastern countries including Jordan enjoy highly aligned development strategies and prominent industrial complementarity. Solid cooperation in traditional sectors has laid a firm foundation for the quality improvement and upgrading of bilateral ties," Zhu Yongbiao, an expert on Middle East affairs at Lanzhou University, told the Global Times. Per data from the Jordan Chamber of Commerce (JCC), in 2025 China became Jordan's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade exceeding $6.7 billion, representing growth of more than 25 percent. The cumulative value of Chinese direct investments implemented in Jordan between 2010 and 2025 exceeded $3.56 billion across 71 projects, according to the JCC, which noted that "these investments have made an important contribution to the Jordanian economy and have helped create thousands of employment opportunities." In an opinion piece in the Ammon News, Jordanian scholar Mahmoud Gudra Anakrih said the relationship with China offers Jordan the possibility of diversifying its economic partnerships at a time when regional instability is making traditional sources of growth increasingly vulnerable. In another opinion piece for the Jordan News, political commentator Nidal Al-Majali said the China-Jordan ties have extended beyond trade to political, economic and strategic cooperation. "Jordan can serve as a bridge between China and the Arab region, rather than merely being an importer of Chinese products," he said. According to Li Xi, an expert from the Center for Jordanian Studies, School of Foreign Studies, Northwestern Polytechnical University, China boasts a complete industrial chain and advanced manufacturing capacity, enabling in‑depth integration of scientific‑technological innovation and industrial development. Meanwhile, Jordan sits at the core hub of the Arab world, with political stability and close ties with regional countries, including Iraq, Israel, Syria and Palestine, allowing it to enjoy unique geopolitical strengths. Jordan's "bridge role" is not merely serving as a transit point for Chinese goods entering Arab markets. More importantly, it can act as a bond for trade, investment, industrial collaboration, people‑to‑people exchanges and regional communication, Li noted. By utilizing Jordan's regional connectivity, China and Arab countries can further realize complementary strengths and win‑win outcomes, said the expert, "This will drive China‑Arab cooperation to expand beyond energy and infrastructure into broader areas including industrial upgrading and scientific‑technological innovation." 2026 marks the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Arab countries, and China is expected to host the second China-Arab States Summit in 2026. A shared strategic choice Four principles should be followed to push for the resolution of the Palestinian question, which is at the heart of the Middle East issue, Xi stressed, Xinhua said. First, a political settlement should be upheld. Second, the principle of "Palestinians governing Palestine" should be followed in advancing the governance of the West Bank and the post-war reconstruction of Gaza. Third, humanitarian principles must be upheld. Fourth, fairness and justice must be upheld, Xi said, per Xinhua. "For Amman, deeper cooperation with Beijing therefore carries both an economic and diplomatic dimension: attracting Chinese capital and expertise while building support among major global powers for Jordan's position on regional security and the Palestinian issue," says The Arab Weekly. Located in the geopolitically volatile Middle East, Jordan is directly affected by the Palestine-Israel conflict, the Syria crisis and other regional security challenges. Its intensified communication with China represents a pragmatic move to pursue steady development amid regional turbulence, Wang noted. "The King's visit enables China and Jordan to bolster strategic communication and coordinate stances on regional flashpoints. It also empowers development cooperation to serve as a pillar of regional stability," Wang said, noting that "the visit carries dual significance: It consolidates bilateral strategic mutual trust and facilitates peace, development and cooperation across the Middle East." Coinciding with King Abdullah II's state visit to China, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi and Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah visited China to hold talks with senior Chinese officials, amid a flurry of Middle‑Eastern diplomatic outreach to China. Taylor Luck, a Middle East correspondent for The Christian Science Monitor, told the Al-Monitor that the significance of the king's visit "lies in its timing." He added that a weeklong visit by the King to China at the time of a deep regional crisis signals a recognition in Jordan that "over-reliance on America is not sustainable in the long term, and increasingly, not even in the short term." "With no end in sight to the war in Iran and an unchecked Israeli policy across the region, the kingdom is hedging against future uncertainty and a less predictable White House," reads the Al-Monitor's report. Wang said the recent spate of high‑level engagements between Middle‑Eastern countries and China demonstrates their growing readiness for China‑related cooperation. Amid shifting international dynamics, regional states value diversified cooperation and strategic autonomy more, and seek less reliance on a single external power. China adheres to mutual respect, non‑interference in internal affairs and mutually beneficial cooperation. It supports Middle‑Eastern countries in pursuing development paths suited to their national conditions and has earned solid political credibility in the region, the expert added. According to Zhu, the so‑called "Looking East" trend should not be viewed as a camp‑alignment move. Rather, it is a pragmatic choice by regional states in pursuit of development, stability and strategic autonomy. "It also shows that China's vision of peaceful development and win‑win cooperation resonates with regional aspiration and is gaining wider recognition," he noted.

item.title: GT Voice: For the prospects of robotics, industry vitality speaks louder than skepticism
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 22:36:00
Visitors watch a robot folding clothes at the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing, August 19, 2026. Photo: VCG As Chinese-made humanoid robots are making spectacular performance at the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG), the commercial prospects of humanoid robots have become a topic of discussion among some Western media outlets. The Economist published an article on Sunday headlined "China will struggle to make money from humanoid robots," which focuses on development challenges such as the high data collection costs facing the sector, casting doubt on the commercial viability of the emerging industry. This perspective does capture the bottlenecks the industry faces in data acquisition and the efficiency of model training. But to judge the commercialization prospects of an emerging industry, one cannot fixate on cost alone. The sustainability of an emerging sector hinges not on temporary bottlenecks, but on the maturity of its industrial ecosystem, richness of application scenarios, and continuous evolution of business models. Take Unitree Robotics, a leading Chinese humanoid robot company, as an example. Unitree's revenue rose to about 1.7 billion yuan ($253 million) in 2025 from 159 million yuan in 2023, with its net profit reaching 288 million yuan in 2025, according to thepaper.cn. More importantly, Unitree's revenue structure has undergone an important change. In 2025, humanoid robots overtook quadruped robots to become Unitree's highest‑revenue product line for the first time. According to its prospectus, the company's humanoid robot revenue reached approximately 877 million yuan in 2025, accounting for more than half of its main business revenue, while actual shipments for the full year exceeded 5,500 units. Profitability at one leading firm does not indicate full industry maturity, but it at least proves the commercial value of humanoid robots within China's robust supply chain and high-quality manufacturing ecosystem. The current skepticism surrounding humanoid robots closely mirrors the doubts that plagued industrial robots in their early days. Yet the global industrial robot industry eventually achieved dramatic cost reductions through large scale adoption in real world scenarios. The commercial path for humanoid robots is not a simple replica of industrial robots. Humanoid robots rely heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) large-language models and require vast amounts of real‑world data or high‑quality simulated training datasets. Their cost structure encompasses not only hardware but also software. Yet, because they are built on an AI foundation, once the core bottlenecks are overcome, their scenario adaptability, application value, and ultimate industrial ceiling will far exceed that of traditional industrial robots. Whether China's robotics industry can achieve commercial viability does not hinge on a single company's financial results, but on the vitality and innovation of the industrial ecosystem. China has more than 1.165 million entities related to the robotics industrial chain, with approximately 144,000 newly added since the beginning of this year. Moreover, the new entrants in the robotics industry are no longer limited to complete machine manufacturers. They are increasingly focused on algorithm development, system integration, scenario specific solutions, software platforms, and engineering services. The trend of integration among robotics and AI, software, and automation systems is becoming more pronounced. Collectively, these developments, spanning manufacturing infrastructure, diverse application demands, technological breakthroughs, and engineering capabilities, have propelled the rapid growth of China's humanoid robot industry and given the country a comprehensive comparative advantage in mass manufacturing and product supply. This systemic advantage is already translating into real-world results. While most global markets are still exploring the possibilities of technology and cost, Chinese companies have already delivered tens of thousands of units in real world scenarios, continuously optimizing performance and cost structures through intense market competition. Data released by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in July showed that more than 400 complete humanoid robot products had been developed in China, accounting for more than half of the global total. According to a report released at the Second WHRG, China shipped more than 40,000 humanoid robots in the first half of 2026, accounting for 97 percent of global shipments. This scale of deployment itself has laid a solid foundation for the commercialization of humanoid robots. While the global market is watching whether humanoid robots can overcome the profitability barrier, China's surging industrial advance is itself the most direct answer.

item.title: Sanae Takaichi must understand the true meaning of 'a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people': Hai Feng
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 19:25:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi responds to questions from party leaders regarding PM Takaichi's policy speech during the House of Councillors plenary session at the Diet building in Tokyo on February 25, 2026. Photo: VCG According to a Japanese media report on August 21, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi recently posted a series of lengthy messages on social media to defend herself against mounting criticism, even quoting the phrase "a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people" from The Analects of Confucius in a desperate bid to rally public support. Japanese political commentators noted that these moves reflect her sense of urgency. Nevertheless, Japanese public opinion is not buying her rhetoric, given her practice of saying one thing but doing another. In her posts, Takaichi claimed that she was mentally prepared for "a certain degree" of criticism, adding, "But 'a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people' - without the trust of the public, a government cannot stand." She also noted that if she cannot gain the public's trust as prime minister, it may hinder the implementation of future policies. Takaichi invoked The Analects of Confucius in an attempt to "limit the damage," but the problem is that she treats this quote merely as a public relations ploy without truly understanding its deeper meaning. "A state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people" is not a shield to be wielded while simultaneously betraying that trust and demanding the public's tolerance. Confucius' maxim was never intended to teach people how to "justify" a breach of trust, but rather how to "prevent" it; it does not address how those in power should defend themselves in the public sphere, but rather what they must do to earn the people's trust. The dictum "a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people" comes from The Analects of Confucius: Yan Yuan. When Zi Gong asked about the way to govern a country, Confucius replied: "Sufficient food, sufficient military preparedness and the trust of the people." Abundant grain supplies, capable national defense and public confidence were the three cornerstones of sound governance. Zi Gong pressed further, asking what should be abandoned first if, out of necessity, one had to give up one of these in turn. Confucius answered "drop military might," and then "drop food supplies." This left the timeless maxim: "Death has always been with us, but a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people." Confucius could not have made the order of priority among food, military strength and trust in the governance of state any clearer; of these three, public trust is the most important. Without military preparedness, a nation faces instability; without food, the people suffer hardship; but once the trust of the people is lost, the government cannot even stand. This is because food ensures survival, military preparedness guarantees security, but only trust sustains the most fundamental political relationship between the state and its people. Therefore, Takaichi's problem today is not merely "why her approval ratings are falling," but rather "why the people no longer trust her." The reasons are not hard to fathom. First, a failure to address people's livelihoods. Surging prices and rising living costs represent the most tangible and immediate source of anxiety in Japanese society. Ordinary people care about their wallets, their incomes and grocery bills - not the countless lengthy posts and explanations churned out on social‑media platforms. With real‑life hardships all too evident, hollow excuses can hardly win over public trust. Second, a failure of self‑reflection. Faced with a continuous decline in approval ratings, if a leader is unwilling to even acknowledge where the problem lies - or worse, adopts an attitude of "I don't know the reason" or "I have nothing to reflect on" - that is not merely a lack of understanding of public sentiment, but a lack of respect for it. The greatest fear in politics is not making mistakes, but making mistakes without realizing it, and clinging to appearances even after losing the people's trust. Third, moral failings in dealing with history. A political figure who truly understands that "a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people" would never repeatedly test the limits on historical issues, much less continuously send the wrong signals on major topics such as the history of aggression, the shadow of militarism, and regional peace and security. As soon as Takaichi took office, she made erroneous remarks regarding Taiwan and has been racing down the dangerous and misguided path of reviving militarism. Being dishonest about history, wavering in her commitment to peace and lacking basic respect for neighboring countries - this "breach of trust" is by no means merely a diplomatic misstep; ultimately, it will also erode her domestic political credibility. Ultimately, Takaichi's problem is that she pays lip service to "trust" while her actions undermine it; she quotes The Analects of Confucius but her conduct runs counter to The Analects of Confucius' principles of governance. She sees only the result - a decline in her approval ratings - but refuses to acknowledge that the cause lies in her own gradual erosion of trust. Ancient Chinese political wisdom has long offered a more profound explanation of this. The Book of History states: "The people are the foundation of a state, and the state will have peace when the foundation is solid." The Words of Mencius goes a step further, asserting: "The people are the most important; the nation is the next; the sovereign is least." In other words, power is not meant to demand understanding from the people. It exists to respond to them, serve them and hold them in reverence. This is the true essence of the saying "a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people." Trust is not a written statement, a citation of classical texts, a string of lengthy posts on social media, or a cultural prop resorted to at the last minute when a crisis strikes. Trust stems from the ruler's integrity, sincerity, sense of responsibility and willingness to correct mistakes and reflect. It comes from keeping the people's hardships close to one's heart and arises from upholding moral boundaries on matters of principle. If Takaichi truly wishes to understand The Analects of Confucius, she should not merely use the phrase "a state cannot stand once it has lost the confidence of the people" to gloss over her own shortcomings. She should first ask herself: Why has she betrayed the trust of her own citizens? Why has she betrayed the trust of neighboring countries? Why has she betrayed the trust of historical justice? This quote from Confucius is by no means an excuse to exonerate her. On the contrary, it serves as a clear mirror that lays bare the true intentions of those in power.

item.title: China, India to hold 25th round of talks on boundary question in Beijing
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 19:03:00
Illustration: Tang Tengfei/GT China and India are scheduled to hold the 25th round of talks between the special representatives on the boundary question in Beijing on Tuesday, and the two sides will discuss the boundary question as well as bilateral, international and regional issues, according to China's Foreign Ministry. Chinese experts said the regular talks signal that bilateral relations are moving toward greater stability and improvement. As agreed between the two sides, Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, and China's Special Representative on the Boundary Question Between China and India Wang Yi will co-chair the 25th Round of Talks Between the Special Representatives on the Boundary Question with India's Special Representative and National Security Advisor Ajit Doval in Beijing on August 25, a spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry announced on Monday. When answering a question about the meeting, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said that the Talks Between the Special Representatives of China and India on the Boundary Question are the main channel for negotiations between China and India on the boundary question, and also an important platform for communication between the two sides on issues of mutual interest. In August last year, China and India successfully held the 24th round of talks, during which the two sides had candid and in-depth exchanges of views on the boundary question and reached a number of common understandings, Lin added. During this round of talks, the two sides will continue the in-depth communication on the boundary question in the spirit of the common understandings between leaders of the two countries to jointly keep the border areas peaceful and tranquil. The two sides will also exchange views on bilateral relations and international and regional issues, the spokesperson said. The 24th Round of Talks Between the Special Representatives of China and India on the Boundary Question was held in New Delhi, India, in August last year. The successive rounds of talks on the China-India boundary question signal that the two sides are advancing boundary negotiations steadily and that bilateral relations are moving toward greater stability and improvement, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times. Ahead of the talks, India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Saturday stressed that peace along the border is essential for improving bilateral ties with China. "I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border areas," Jaishankar said at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum in New Delhi, according to the Indian Express. "At the end of the day, peace and tranquility in the border areas is a prerequisite for good relations, and the state of the border, to a very large measure, naturally would determine the state of the relations," he said. Responding to questions from Bloomberg and Reuters concerning social media claims about stepped-up Chinese military activity and an Indian government spokesman also not denying that a new border incident had occurred, Guo Jiakun, spokesperson from China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on August 12 that "The China-India border situation is generally stable at the moment. China and India held the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs last week. The two sides agreed to maintain communication via diplomatic and military channels and jointly uphold peace and tranquility in the border areas." Despite the positive momentum of bilateral engagement, Indian side has still taken provocative moves along the border. India on August 7 announced what it called "standard" names for 27 locations in so-called "Arunachal Pradesh," a move that some Indian media outlets portrayed as an effort to counter China and further linked to the latest reports of border tensions. Responding to the issue on August 10, spokesperson Guo said, "Zangnan region is China's territory. China does not recognize the so-called 'Arunachal Pradesh' illegally set up by India." The past rounds of talks between the Special Representatives on the China-India Boundary Question have demonstrated that the two countries have the capacity to manage border issues, Hu Zhiyong, Director of the Center for India Studies, Distinguished Professor at Zhejiang International Studies University and a research fellow at the Institute of International Relations at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. If India is sincere in creating a friendly atmosphere for the upcoming BRICS Summit, it should avoid creating new disputes over border issues, as doing so would neither help resolve existing differences nor contribute to the improvement of bilateral relations, Hu said.

item.title: Typhoon Atsani forms as Narra suspends trains in Guangxi: Why is typhoon activity unusually high this year?
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 16:51:00
Rescue personnel use boats to evacuate residents to safety after flooding hit a town in Ningming county, South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on August 23, 2026, following the impact of a typhoon. Photo: VCG China's National Commission for Disaster Prevention, Reduction and Relief and the Ministry of Emergency Management activated a Level-IV national disaster relief emergency response for South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region on Monday after Typhoon Narra, the 19th typhoon of this year, caused severe flooding in the region that led to passenger train suspensions. A working group was sent to the affected areas to assess damage and assist with evacuations, resettlement and basic relief efforts, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Monday. The China Meteorological Administration raised its emergency response for major weather disasters, including typhoons, torrential rain and severe convective weather, to Level III at 11:50 am on Monday. China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) continued to issue a yellow alert for rainstorm and a blue alert for typhoon at 6 am on Monday, forecasting torrential rainfall in parts of coastal regions as well as Liaoning and Heilongjiang provinces. The rainfall on Taiwan Island is forecast to reach 250 to 300 millimeters between Monday morning and Tuesday morning, CCTV reported. Typhoon Narra was located over the Beibu Gulf about 185 kilometers west-southwest of Beihai, Guangxi, at 5 am on Monday, with maximum winds of 23 meters per second near its center. It is expected to linger over the Beibu Gulf and strengthen to severe tropical storm, with winds of up to 25 to 28 meters per second. From Monday night, it will turn northward and move at 5 to 10 kilometers per hour toward the coast from Guangxi to western Leizhou Peninsula in South China's Guangdong Province. Meanwhile, Typhoon Atsani, the year's 21st typhoon, formed Monday morning. Its center was located about 1,970 kilometers east-southeast of Taipei of the Taiwan Island at 8 am, and is expected to move north-northeast at 15 to 20 kilometers per hour, with little change in its strength, CCTV reported. Rescue personnel use boats to evacuate residents to safety after flooding hit a county in Fangchenggang city, South China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on August 23, 2026, following the impact of a typhoon. Photo: VCG Due to the impact of Typhoon Narra, Ningming county in Guangxi is forecast to see moderate to heavy rain and locally torrential rain from Wednesday to Thursday. In response to typhoon, heavy rainfall and flood warnings, multiple passenger train services have been suspended from Sunday to Thursday, according to CCTV. According to Zhang Ling, a chief weather forecaster at the NMC, Typhoon Narra remains stalled over the Beibu Gulf as several surrounding weather systems compete to steer the storm, with none dominant. Meanwhile, warm waters and abundant monsoon moisture are helping Typhoon Narra persist, bringing prolonged rain and strong winds to southern China's coast, the Beibu Gulf and the northern South China Sea. Rescue personnel use boats to evacuate residents to safety after flooding hit a county in Fangchenggang city, South China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, on August 23, 2026, following the impact of a typhoon. Photo: VCG On Saturday, Fangchenggang in Guangxi recorded a maximum accumulated rainfall of 404.9 millimeters. As more rain is expected in Guangxi and other areas, attention should be paid to the cumulative effects of prolonged rainfall, with southern Guangxi facing heightened risks from heavy cumulative rainfall and intense short-duration downpours, Zhang told the Global Times on Monday. According to Ma Jun, director of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, 21 typhoons have formed over the western North Pacific and South China Sea this year, nine more than the historical average for the same period. The surge in activity is closely related to the current super El Nino conditions. During an El Nino event, hurricane activity in the Atlantic tends to be suppressed, resulting in fewer storms, while typhoon activity in the western Pacific tends to increase. The number of typhoons formed so far this year is consistent with the typical pattern of typhoon activity during an El Nino year, Ma told the Global Times on Monday.

item.title: China's cyberspace regulator intensifies crackdown on group livestream misconduct
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 13:44:00
Photo of group livestream. Photo: VCG China's cyberspace regulator has shut down more than 7,200 illegal group livestreaming rooms and penalized over 2,200 accounts as part of an intensified crackdown on misconduct in online group livestreaming entertainment. The campaign targets vulgar content, mechanisms designed to encourage excessive tipping, and infringements on minors' rights. The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) has also instructed online platforms to remove or take action against a number of MCN agencies involved in serious misconduct, issued 17 notices on the campaign, and publicized typical cases to deter further violations, said regulator on its WeChat account. During a campaign, the CAC has sought to combine enforcement with tighter regulation by improving content review, adjusting ranking systems and interactive features, and strengthening oversight of group livestreaming accounts and MCN agencies. Online platforms have also been urged to assume greater responsibility for managing such content. Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, has begun displaying information about affiliated MCN agencies on group livestreaming accounts and has organized training for agencies to curb misconduct at the source. Kuaishou, one of China's popular short-video platforms, has refined its review standards and strengthened technical tools to better identify vulgar content and inappropriate interactions. WeChat Channels have introduced an identity-verification mechanism for suspected underage participants in group livestreams with the aim to preventing minors from appearing in such broadcasts in disguised or less obvious ways. Bilibili, a Chinese video platform, meanwhile, has removed features such as multiplier points, tiered bonuses and ranking competitions that could encourage viewers to spend money on virtual gifts. Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, Chinese equivalent of Instagram, has imposed measures including traffic restrictions to curb practices such as repetitive shouting and livestreaming competitions that lack substantive content. The CAC said that the campaign has led to a significant decline in vulgar content in entertainment group livestreaming, while violations involving the inducement of excessive tipping have been effectively curbed. The regulator said it will maintain strict oversight, intensify action against accounts and agencies that violate regulations, and push online platforms to improve management mechanisms and technological capabilities. It will also continue to optimize livestreaming features to foster a healthier and more orderly online entertainment environment. Global Times

item.title: Two Chinese sailors rescued, 22 missing after Panama-flagged bulk carrier sinks off eastern India's coast; operation still ongoing: embassy tells GT
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 10:16:00
Caption: The Indian Coast Guard and the Indian Navy have launched a joint rescue operation after the Panama-flagged bulk carrier Ocean Winner sank in waters off the coast of Paradip, India's Odisha state. Photo: Screenshot of NDTV's report Two Chinese sailors have been rescued after a Panama-flagged bulk carrier carrying 24 crew members sank in the Bay of Bengal, about 230 nautical miles off the coast of Paradip, India's Odisha state, as Indian authorities intensified search-and-rescue operations for the remaining 22 crew members, according to multiple Indian media outlets and Reuters. The two sailors were rescued from life rafts by MT Aisopos, a commercial vessel operating nearby, after an Indian Navy P-8I maritime surveillance aircraft located the rafts during the search-and-rescue mission, the Times of India reported. The Chinese embassy in India told the Global Times that the rescue operation is still ongoing. The two Chinese seafarers said the vessel, called Ocean Winner, had developed a list on Friday and sank within eight minutes, forcing the crew to abandon ship, Reuters reported, citing Shyam Jagannathan, director general of India's Maritime Administration. Jagannathan said the chances of finding survivors generally fall sharply after the first 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing their search. "All agencies are coordinating closely and actively doing search and rescue efforts," Sarbananda Sonowal, federal minister for India's Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, said in a social media post, according to Reuters. India has experience and capabilities in maritime rescue operations in the Indian Ocean, and the practice is part of the country's international humanitarian responsibilities. Yet its active efforts to rescue the Chinese crew members could still leave a positive impression among Chinese people and allow the public to feel India's goodwill, which may improve China-India relations, Lin Minwang, deputy director of the Center for South Asian Studies at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Monday. Having relevant officials continue to follow up on the rescue efforts and convey goodwill could further demonstrate India's willingness to improve ties with China, Lin said. Ocean Winner, with IMO number 9145530, was a 70,000-deadweight-ton bulk carrier built in 1998. It loaded iron ore at Paradip and departed for Singapore on Thursday with 24 crew members aboard, according to Maritime Executive. The vessel's Automatic Identification System signal disappeared in the middle of the Bay of Bengal at 4:45 pm GMT on Friday. The crew issued a distress alert at around the same time, the report said. India has long sought the role of a security provider in the Indian Ocean and a major regional power. When maritime emergencies occur in the region, the Indian Navy and Coast Guard are capable of providing relatively timely assistance, Lin added. The 22 missing crew members include 18 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard. Two Coast Guard vessels were dispatched from Sri Vijaya Puram, formerly known as Port Blair and the capital of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands, to join the search-and-rescue operation, according to a Coast Guard spokesperson cited by Reuters. Separately, Maritime Executive noted that iron ore fines can become hazardous when wet, as the cargo may liquefy and suddenly shift to one side while a vessel is rolling. This induces a list, accompanied by free surface effect, with serious adverse impact on stability. From 2007 to 2019, 29 seafarers were killed in casualties involving iron ore cargoes, the outlet reported.

item.title: Chinese teenagers flock to tech frontline to touch the future amid AI study-tour boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24 08:42:00
Children participate in a robot football competition in Jiyuan City, central China's Henan Province, Aug. 15, 2026. (Photo by Duan Erping/Xinhua) On a summer day, cheers erupted as clusters of children watched robots race across a soccer pitch, battling it out in playful matches, at a science center in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province. At a nearby workbench, nine-year-old Zhang Qihang was busy assembling a robot of his own. "Building robots is awesome! I can let my imagination run wild," he said, beaming with excitement. This was the scene at an artificial intelligence (AI) summer camp -- part of a new wave of study tours gaining traction across China. Moving beyond textbooks, students are flocking to tech giants, university labs and science centers, eager to get hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI technologies and see firsthand how the future is taking shape. A volunteer (2nd L) instructs a child how to assemble a robot in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, July 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ziheng) AI STUDY-TOUR BOOM During this summer vacation, AI-themed study tours have begun to gain ground, with bookings surging 370 percent year on year, according to online travel platform Ctrip. To tap into the growing demand for AI-focused tech tourism, a travel agency based in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, began adding visits to technology companies to its trip programs last summer. "On our Shanghai-Hangzhou independent study tours, AI-related activities now account for more than 80 percent of the itinerary," founder Zhu Ping said. The boom is unfolding against the backdrop of China's broader AI boom, powered by a wave of homegrown models and applications. For a growing number of Chinese teenagers, AI tools such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Doubao are becoming familiar companions in their everyday lives. The number of AI enterprises in China had surpassed 6,000 last year, and the output value of the core AI industry was projected to exceed 1.2 trillion yuan (about 177 billion U.S. dollars) during the same period, representing a year-on-year increase of nearly 30 percent. Moreover, China was home to more than 140 humanoid robot developers in 2025, with shipments reaching 14,400 units -- accounting for 84.7 percent of the global market, according to an industry research report. To help children prepare for an AI-driven future, China unveiled an "AI Plus Education" initiative earlier this year, encouraging schools to take AI learning beyond the classroom through after-school programs and hands-on activities. The goal is to help students understand and use AI properly, while sparking curiosity, nurturing creativity and honing their critical-thinking and problem-solving skills. Today, the AI study-tour wave is sweeping through China's schools, as primary and secondary schools incorporate it into their educational programs. Parents are taking their children into the heart of the tech industry to see how AI transforms the real world. China's tech-tourism boom is also drawing international visitors keen to get a close-up look at the innovation behind "Made in China." Since opening in Shanghai in May, Unitree Robotics's first embodied intelligence experience store in Asia has attracted many foreign visitors. Victoria, from Denmark, visited the store last month. "I've seen some of the dancing videos, but it's really cool to see them in real life," she said, viewing the development of AI and robotics in China as "revolutionary, new and exciting." A Russian tourist interacts with a robot at a store of Unitree Robotics in Beijing, capital of China, April 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong) FROM AI USERS TO AI CREATORS Today's children are growing up as AI natives, already fluent in AI tools. But AI study camps are opening a new window onto how the technology is reshaping the world around them and how they can use it to make a difference. For Liang Yiduo, a Beijing middle school student, an AI summer camp run by internet giant NetEase offered a fresh perspective on the AI technology he thought he already knew. "I realized that large language models aren't just chatbots or simple tools," he said. "They can be assistants that work alongside you and help you create things tailored to your needs, like 'claws.'" "The goal of the study camp is to help children move from simply using AI to understanding it, creating with it and even building their own AI agents," said Wang Lijin, director and founder of Beijing Venus Future Education Consulting Center, which assists NetEase in running its study camps. Students attending a summer camp control a robot at an AI robot technology experience center in Shanghai, east China, July 19, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Xu/Xinhua) Some study tour organizers design programs around students' interests and abilities, aiming to spark curiosity and encourage deeper thinking. Shanghai Qingbao Robot Co., Ltd., for example, offers students who enjoy building things the chance to assemble robotic arms and explore the mechanics of shoulder and neck structures. It also gives students a comparative look at the robotics and AI industries in China, the US, Europe and Japan, helping them gain a more balanced understanding of China's strengths and shortcomings. Wang Lei, the company's chairman, believes that study tours can greatly broaden students' horizons in science and innovation. "Through immersive study tours, students start thinking for themselves about how robotics can be applied to everyday life, from unmanned retail to automated pharmacies," he said. Some students are taking it a step further, learning to spot real-world problems and use AI to develop solutions. In the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, a group of students spent six days in a camp turning ideas into an AI-powered product. "I've realized that learning AI isn't about showing off what I can do with it, but about using it to solve real problems for others," said one team member. "I want to keep learning AI so I can help more people in the future."
